name: Chronic Respiratory Insufficiency

conventional_description:
Chronic respiratory insufficiency is the inability of the lungs to adequately exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, leading to persistent shortness of breath, fatigue, and reduced exercise tolerance. It often results from long-term lung conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pulmonary fibrosis, or severe asthma, where lung tissue is damaged or airways are obstructed.
Diagnosis typically involves pulmonary function tests, chest imaging, and arterial blood gas analysis to measure oxygen and carbon dioxide levels. The condition is progressive and can significantly impact quality of life, often requiring ongoing medical management.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments aim to relieve symptoms and slow progression. They include bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids to open airways, supplemental oxygen therapy for low blood oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation to improve stamina, and in advanced cases, lung transplantation. Medications are often taken daily, and oxygen may be needed continuously.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, chronic respiratory insufficiency is understood as a profound deficiency of Qi and fluids that causes the Lungs to wither and lose their ability to descend and diffuse breath. The condition is called fèi wěi (lung atrophy), and it is never just a Lung problem. The Spleen must generate the Qi that fuels the Lungs, and the Kidneys must grasp the inhaled air and anchor it deep in the body. When these organ systems are weakened over months or years - by illness, overwork, poor diet, or constitutional vulnerability - the Lungs are left unsupported and gradually fail.
This is why the same Western diagnosis can have many different TCM faces. One person may have a dry, hacking cough with thirst and a red tongue, pointing to Lung Dryness from fluid loss. Another may feel breathless after eating, with bloating and loose stools, revealing Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. A third may have shallow, effort-induced panting with a sore lower back and night sweats, indicating Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. A fourth pattern, Kidneys failing to receive Qi, makes the breath even shallower - a feeling that no matter how hard you try, the air never reaches deep enough. Lung Yang Deficiency brings a cold chest, watery frothy sputum, and deep fatigue. And Phlegm obstruction can settle on top of any deficiency, causing chest heaviness and copious sticky sputum. Each pattern reflects a different root, and each requires a different treatment strategy - cooling and moistening for dryness, strengthening the middle for digestive weakness, deeply nourishing for Yin depletion, warming and grasping for Kidney failure, or transforming phlegm for obstruction.
TCM diagnosis uses the quality of the breath, the nature of the cough and sputum, and the tongue and pulse to untangle which layers of deficiency and excess are present, so treatment can be precisely targeted.
classical_quote: 「寸口脉数，其人咳，口中反有浊唾涎沫者何？师曰：为肺痿之病。」
classical_translation: "When the cun pulse is rapid, the patient coughs, and there is turbid saliva and frothy sputum in the mouth - what is that? The master says: It is the disease of lung atrophy."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about the nature of the breathlessness, the cough, and any sputum. The quality of these clues-dry or productive, worse with activity or at rest-points toward one of several patterns. The tongue and pulse are then checked to confirm the diagnosis, because each pattern leaves a distinct imprint on these mirrors of the body’s inner condition.
If the chief complaint is a dry, hacking cough with scanty, sticky sputum that is hard to bring up, accompanied by thirst and a sensation of heat, the pattern is likely Lung Dryness. The tongue will appear red with a yellow coat, and the pulse feels thin and rapid. This reflects Lung Heat consuming fluids, which is a frequent early-stage picture in lung atrophy.
When gradual shortness of breath and fatigue dominate, along with poor appetite, loose stools, and a washed-out complexion, the practitioner suspects Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak. Here the digestive system fails to generate enough Qi to support the Lungs, so the breathing weakness is paired with digestive sluggishness.
Soreness in the lower back and knees, dizziness, tinnitus, and night sweats point toward Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. Long-standing lung disease depletes these deep reserves, and the respiratory weakness deepens as the body’s cooling, moistening resources run low.
If the breath feels shallow and the person struggles to inhale, especially after even mild exertion, the pattern is Kidneys failing to receive Qi. The Kidneys lose their ability to grasp the Qi and pull it downward, so the breath never feels full. The tongue may be pale, and the pulse is often deep and weak.
When the person feels constantly cold, with chilly limbs, watery white sputum, and an aversion to cold, Lung Yang Deficiency is likely. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep and weak. This pattern often appears in later stages when the warming, activating force of Yang has been damaged and cold-phlegm obstructs the Lungs.
A sense of chest oppression with copious, thick, difficult-to-clear sputum indicates Phlegm obstructing the Lung collaterals. The tongue coating is greasy, and the pulse is slippery. Phlegm rarely stands alone-it frequently complicates the deficiency patterns above, adding a sticky, congested layer to an already weakened respiratory system.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry, hacking cough with scanty or no phlegm", "Persistent dryness of the mouth, nose, and throat", "Dry, cracked lips and skin", "Thirst with a desire to drink", "Mild fever and aversion to wind"]
patterns.worse_with: Dry, heated indoor air, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Smoking or smoky air, Excessive talking, Windy weather
patterns.better_with: Cool, moist air, Warm drinks and soups, Rest in a humid environment, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: When external dryness or heat invades the Lungs, it rapidly consumes the thin, moist fluids that keep the lung tissue supple and functional. Without this moisture, the Lungs become parched and unable to properly descend and diffuse Qi. Over time, this fluid loss causes the lung tissue to wither and atrophy, which is the very essence of lung atrophy (肺痿).
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a dry surface and a thin white or thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: floating (fú) and rapid (shuò), or fine (xì).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Dryness is a condition of fluid depletion in the Lungs. Dry, heated, or smoky air directly evaporates the Lung's moisture, while spicy and fried foods generate internal heat that consumes Yin. Wind also dries. Conversely, cool, moist air and warm fluids help replenish the lost Yin and soothe the dry tissues. Rest and gentle breathing reduce the demand on Lung Qi, allowing the body to conserve and rebuild fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of warm fluids like pear juice or honey-lemon water. Avoid dry, spicy, or fried foods that consume fluids. Use a humidifier in dry environments. Gentle breathing exercises can help maintain lung moisture.

patterns.symptoms: ["Poor appetite and early fullness", "Abdominal bloating after meals", "Loose stools", "Fatigue and heavy, weak limbs", "Sallow or pale complexion", "Shortness of breath after eating or when tired"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or eating late, Cold, raw foods and drinks, Excessive worry and overthinking, Physical overexertion, Damp, humid weather
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Warm, cooked meals, Small, frequent meals, Gentle abdominal massage, Warm environment
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Stomach are the body's engine for making Qi from food. When they are weak, not enough Qi is produced to keep the Lungs strong and the breath deep. This leaves you short of breath, especially after eating or any exertion, because the body simply lacks the fuel to power the respiratory muscles. Over time, the poor digestion and loose stools also deprive the Lungs of the nourishment they need to heal, making the respiratory weakness chronic.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, with tooth marks on the sides and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and especially empty at the right middle position (Spleen/Stomach).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and routine. Overeating, cold foods, and mental strain all weaken its ability to transform food into Qi, directly worsening the deficiency that underlies the breathing difficulty. Rest and easily digested meals conserve Qi, allowing the body to redirect energy toward respiration and recovery.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Eat small, frequent meals to avoid overburdening digestion. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi flow without exhausting the body.

patterns.symptoms: ["Shortness of breath on exertion", "Lower back ache and weakness", "Dizziness and ringing in the ears", "Night sweats with heat in palms and soles", "Dry mouth and throat with dry cough", "Afternoon flushed cheeks"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and sleep deprivation, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Stress and frustration, Hot, dry environments
patterns.better_with: Rest and early nights, Cool, moist air, Moistening foods (pear, congee), Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the root of Qi and must grasp the air we breathe. When Kidney Yin is depleted, the Kidneys fail to anchor Qi, so breath becomes shallow and exertion quickly brings on panting. The Liver stores Blood and ensures smooth flow; its Yin deficiency lets heat rise, which further parches the Lungs and dries their tissues. Over time, the Lungs lose their moisture and elasticity, leading to the characteristic wasting and weakness of chronic respiratory insufficiency.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, thin and possibly cracked, with little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin), rapid, and often wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position is weak and deep.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, nourishing substance. Overwork, late nights, and stress consume Yin and generate heat, which further dries the Lungs and weakens the Kidneys' ability to grasp Qi. Rest, cooling temperatures, and moistening foods replenish Yin and calm deficiency fire, allowing the Lungs to be rehydrated and the breath to deepen.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritise rest and avoid overwork, especially late nights. Eat small, frequent meals of moistening, yin-nourishing foods such as pear, black sesame, goji berries, and congee. Steer clear of spicy, fried, or drying foods and alcohol. Gentle practices like tai chi or restorative yoga help preserve Yin.

patterns.symptoms: ["Easier to breathe out than in", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Lower back ache and weakness", "Fatigue and weak voice"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or drafts, Physical overexertion, Standing for long periods, Fear and chronic anxiety
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Warmth on the lower back, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic respiratory insufficiency, the Lungs have been weakened over a long period. The Kidneys are meant to anchor the breath by grasping the Qi that the Lungs draw in. When Kidney Qi is depleted, this grasping power fails, so each inhalation feels shallow and incomplete-the air never seems to go deep enough. The effort of breathing exhausts the body further, and the lack of deep, anchored breath accelerates the decline of the already weakened Lungs, creating a vicious cycle where the breath becomes more and more superficial with the slightest activity.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and puffy with teeth marks, and a thin white moist coating. Pulse: deep and weak, especially feeble at the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Kidneys govern the body’s deepest reserves of Qi and are easily drained by cold, overwork, and fear. Resting conserves that Qi, and warmth directly supports the Kidney Yang that is needed to receive and anchor the breath. Exertion and standing force the body to use up the Qi that should be holding the breath steady, while fear, the emotion associated with the Kidneys, further depletes them and makes the breathing even more shallow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower back and feet warm, and avoid cold or raw foods that chill the interior. Gentle movement like tai chi or slow walking can strengthen the Kidneys without depleting Qi. Simple pursed-lip breathing exercises help train the body to exhale fully and make space for a deeper inhalation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Thin, watery, frothy white sputum", "Cold sensation in chest and upper back", "Cold hands and feet, aversion to cold", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Pale, puffy tongue with teeth marks"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw foods and drinks, Cold, damp weather, Physical overexertion, Prolonged sadness or grief
patterns.better_with: Warm drinks and soups, Keeping the chest warm, Gentle rest and relaxation, Moxibustion on the upper back
patterns.why_this_happens: When Lung Yang is weakened, the warming and transforming functions of the Lungs fail. This allows thin, watery fluids to accumulate as cold-phlegm, which blocks the airways and causes a chronic cough with frothy white sputum. The chest and back feel cold because Yang cannot warm the upper body, and every breath feels shallow because the Lungs lack the power to descend and distribute Qi properly.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and moist with teeth marks; thin white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially weak at the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and raw foods, along with cold environments, further deplete the already weak Lung Yang, making it harder to transform fluids and warm the chest. Overexertion drains Qi and Yang, while grief can stagnate Lung Qi, worsening the deficiency. Warmth, rest, and gentle movement conserve Yang and help Qi flow, while moxibustion directly delivers warming energy to the Lungs and their supporting organs.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the chest and back warm with layers, and avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks entirely. Eat warm, cooked meals like soups and stews with gentle spices such as ginger and cinnamon. Gentle breathing exercises and short walks can help move Qi, but rest is essential when fatigue sets in.

patterns.why_this_happens: Phlegm is a thick, turbid substance that forms when the Spleen fails to transform fluids properly. In chronic respiratory insufficiency, this sticky Phlegm settles in the Lungs, clogging the airways and obstructing the flow of Qi. The result is a heavy, oppressive sensation in the chest, a productive cough with copious sputum, and worsening shortness of breath because the Lungs cannot expand and descend properly.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: swollen pale body with tooth marks, thick white greasy coating, moist. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), smooth and rolling like beads.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is formed when the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, leading to an accumulation of Dampness that congeals into turbid Phlegm. Damp, heavy, and cold foods, as well as humid environments, add to this Dampness burden. Warm, dry foods and gentle movement help the Spleen to function and transform Phlegm, while avoiding damp-producing items prevents further buildup.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid damp-producing foods like dairy, sugar, fried foods, and cold raw vegetables. Favor warm, cooked meals with mild spices like ginger and cardamom. Gentle daily exercise helps move Qi and transform Dampness, but avoid overexertion that depletes Qi.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help chronic shortness of breath?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially when the breathlessness is due to a deficiency pattern that conventional medicine doesn't address. TCM works by strengthening the organs that support breathing - the Spleen, Kidneys, and Lungs themselves - and by clearing phlegm or dryness that obstructs the airways. Many patients find their stamina improves, their reliance on rescue inhalers decreases, and their overall energy returns. It is a gradual process, not a quick fix, but for chronic conditions it can make a meaningful difference.

faqs.question: How long until I notice a difference?
faqs.answer: Most people notice subtle improvements in energy and sleep within the first 4-8 weeks. Breathing capacity may take longer to improve, often 3-6 months. The timeline depends on the pattern: Spleen Qi deficiency tends to respond faster, while deep Kidney depletion requires more time. Consistency is key - daily herbs and weekly acupuncture produce the best results.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my inhalers and oxygen?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be safely combined with conventional treatments. Herbs and acupuncture do not interfere with bronchodilators or inhaled steroids, and they can be used together with oxygen therapy. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your pulmonologist about all treatments you are using. Never stop prescribed medications or oxygen without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. In general, warm, cooked foods are easier to digest and help generate Qi. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Depending on your pattern, specific foods may be recommended - for example, pears and lily bulbs for Lung Dryness, or ginger and cinnamon for cold patterns. Your practitioner will guide you on the best choices.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe if I have a serious lung condition?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is very safe when performed by a licensed practitioner. Needles are sterile and single-use, and points are often chosen on the back, chest, and limbs. If you have fragile skin or are on blood thinners, inform your acupuncturist so they can adjust their technique. Acupuncture should not be performed over areas of active infection or skin breakdown.

faqs.question: What if my condition is very severe - can TCM still help?
faqs.answer: Even in advanced stages, TCM can improve quality of life by reducing fatigue, easing breathlessness, and supporting appetite and sleep. It may not reverse structural lung damage, but it can strengthen the body's remaining capacity and help you feel more comfortable. Many patients use TCM alongside conventional care to manage symptoms and maintain independence.

research.title: Expert consensus on TCM diagnosis and treatment of lung atrophy (Fei Wei) in Jiangxi Province
research.description: A provincial expert consensus that standardizes the TCM pattern differentiation, treatment principles, and representative formulas for lung atrophy. It identifies key patterns such as Lung Dryness, Spleen-Stomach Qi Deficiency, and Kidney-Liver Yin Deficiency, and recommends formulas like Qing Zao Jiu Fei Tang and Wen Fei Hua Xian Tang.
